title: Les conditionnelles mixtes / Mixed conditionals
bridge: In Spanish, mixed conditionals (like 'si hubiera sabido, no lo haría') combine tenses flexibly, and French does something similar, but with important nuances. The main difference is that in French, tense agreement in the 'si' clause is stricter: the conditional is never used after 'si', but rather the imperfect or pluperfect indicative. Furthermore, French clearly distinguishes between hypothetical situations affecting the present or future and those affecting the past, whereas in Spanish they sometimes overlap.
rule: In French, mixed conditionals combine a past condition (pluperfect) with a present or future consequence (present conditional), or vice versa: a present condition (imperfect) with a past consequence (past conditional). The basic structure is: 'Si + pluperfect, + present conditional' (e.g., 'Si j'avais su, je le ferais') or 'Si + imperfect, + past conditional' (e.g., 'Si j'étais riche, j'aurais acheté cette maison'). The conditional is never used in the 'si' clause. Structures without 'si' can also be used, such as 'Avoir pu + infinitive' or 'Sans + noun/participle', to express counterfactual hypotheses. For B2, it is essential to master tense agreement, the use of 'si' with imperfect/pluperfect, and the difference between real and unreal hypotheses.

common_error.wrong: Si j'aurais su, je serais venu.
common_error.correct: Si j'avais su, je serais venu.
common_error.explanation: This is a very common mistake because in Spanish you say 'si hubiera sabido' and the conditional in Spanish is 'habría', but in French, after 'si', the conditional is never used; instead, the imperfect or pluperfect indicative is used. To avoid it, remember that 'si' requires the indicative (imperfect or pluperfect) and only the main verb takes the conditional.

examples.original: Si j'avais le temps, je t'aiderais.
examples.phonetic: si ʒ‿avɛ lə tɑ̃ ʒə t‿ɛdʁɛ
examples.translation: If I had time, I would help you.
examples.note: Condition in the present (imperfect) and consequence in the present (simple conditional).

examples.note: Past condition (pluperfect) and past result (past conditional).

examples.translation: If you had come, you would have met Marie.
examples.note: Imperfect 'étais' indicates an unrealized past action, with a hypothetical result in the past.

examples.phonetic: si nu avjɔ̃ sy nu səʁjɔ̃ paʁti ply to
examples.translation: If we had known, we would have left earlier.
examples.note: Use of 'serions partis' (past conditional of 'partir') with agreement of the past participle.

examples.note: Literary construction without 'si', with compound infinitive.

examples.translation: If I had studied, I would be able to do it now.
examples.note: Mix of past condition with present result (simple conditional).

examples.phonetic: si ty etɛ paʁti ply to ty nə səʁɛ pa fatige mɛ̃tənɑ̃
examples.translation: If you had left earlier, you wouldn't be tired now.
examples.note: Mix: past condition, present result.

title: La voix passive avancée / Advanced passive voice
bridge: In Spanish, the passive voice with 'ser' + participle is common, but in French it is even more frequent and has important nuances. Unlike Spanish, where the reflexive passive ('se vende') is sometimes used, French prefers the passive with 'être'. Furthermore, French requires agreement of the past participle with the subject in gender and number, something that is not always visible in Spanish. Be careful with compound tenses: in French, 'être' is used as the auxiliary in the passive, not 'avoir'.
rule: The passive voice in French is formed with the verb 'être' (in the appropriate tense) + past participle of the main verb. The participle agrees in gender and number with the subject. To express the agent, 'par' is used (or 'de' with verbs of feeling). Compound tenses of the passive require a double auxiliary: the auxiliary of the compound tense of 'être' + participle of 'être' + past participle. With modals (devoir, pouvoir, vouloir), the passive is formed with the modal + être + participle. Passive gerunds and infinitives are constructed with 'étant' + participle and 'être' + participle respectively. Examples: 'La maison est construite' (present), 'La maison a été construite' (compound past), 'La maison sera construite' (future), 'La maison doit être construite' (modal).

concept_examples.text: Le rapport est rédigé par le directeur.
concept_examples.translation: The report is written by the director.
concept_examples.phonetic: /lə ʁa.pɔʁ ɛ ʁe.di.ʒe paʁ lə di.ʁɛk.tœʁ/

concept_examples.text: Les lettres ont été envoyées hier.
concept_examples.translation: The letters were sent yesterday.
concept_examples.phonetic: /le lɛtʁ ɔ̃ te ɑ̃.vwa.je jɛʁ/

concept_examples.text: Ce travail doit être terminé avant vendredi.
concept_examples.translation: This work must be finished before Friday.
concept_examples.phonetic: /sə tʁa.vaj dwa ɛtʁ tɛʁ.mi.ne a.vɑ̃ vɑ̃.dʁə.di/

concept_examples.text: En étant bien préparé, on réussit.
concept_examples.translation: Being well prepared, one succeeds.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɑ̃ e.tɑ̃ bjɛ̃ pʁe.pa.ʁe ɔ̃ ʁe.y.si/

common_error.wrong: La maison a construite par les ouvriers.
common_error.correct: La maison a été construite par les ouvriers.
common_error.correct_alt: La maison est construite par les ouvriers.
common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish 'la casa ha construida' is said in some dialects or the participle of 'être' is omitted. In French, the passive always requires the auxiliary 'être' in the appropriate tense. For the compound past, the auxiliary 'avoir' in its form 'a' + participle of 'être' ('été') + past participle of the main verb is needed. Avoid using 'avoir' directly with the participle of the main verb without the 'été'.

examples.original: Le gâteau est mangé par les enfants.
examples.phonetic: /lə ɡɑ.to ɛ mɑ̃.ʒe paʁ le zɑ̃.fɑ̃/
examples.translation: The cake is eaten by the children.
examples.note: Present passive: 'être' in present + past participle. Agreement: 'mangé' (masculine singular) because 'gâteau' is masculine singular.

examples.original: Les chansons étaient chantées par la foule.
examples.phonetic: /le ʃɑ̃.sɔ̃ e.tɛ ʃɑ̃.te paʁ la ful/
examples.translation: The songs were sung by the crowd.
examples.note: Imperfect passive: 'étaient' + participle. Agreement: 'chantées' (feminine plural) because 'chansons' is feminine plural.

examples.original: La porte sera fermée à dix heures.
examples.phonetic: /la pɔʁt sə.ʁa fɛʁ.me a diz œʁ/
examples.translation: The door will be closed at ten o'clock.
examples.note: Future passive: 'sera' + participle. Agreement: 'fermée' (feminine singular).

examples.original: Les devoirs ont été faits par les élèves.
examples.phonetic: /le də.vwaʁ ɔ̃ te fɛ paʁ le zɛ.lɛv/
examples.translation: The homework has been done by the students.
examples.note: Compound past: 'ont été' + participle. Double auxiliary: avoir + été + participle. Agreement: 'faits' (masculine plural).

examples.original: La décision avait été prise avant la réunion.
examples.phonetic: /la de.si.zjɔ̃ a.vɛ te pʁiz a.vɑ̃ la ʁe.y.njɔ̃/
examples.translation: The decision had been made before the meeting.
examples.note: Pluperfect: 'avait été' + participle. Agreement: 'prise' (feminine singular because of 'décision').

examples.original: Les résultats seront annoncés demain.
examples.phonetic: /le ʁe.zyl.ta sə.ʁɔ̃ a.nɔ̃.se də.mɛ̃/
examples.translation: The results will be announced tomorrow.
examples.note: Future perfect passive: 'seront annoncés' – not compound but shows agreement. Careful: simple future of 'être' + participle.

levels.label: Passif avec modaux, infinitif et gérondif
levels.translation: Passive with modals, infinitive and gerund

examples.original: Ce problème peut être résolu facilement.
examples.phonetic: /sə pʁɔ.blɛm pø ɛtʁ ʁe.zɔ.ly fa.sil.mɑ̃/
examples.translation: This problem can be solved easily.
examples.note: Modal (peut) + passive infinitive (être + participle). No agreement with the subject in the infinitive.

examples.original: Les règles doivent être respectées par tous.
examples.phonetic: /le ʁɛɡl dwav ɛtʁ ʁɛs.pɛk.te paʁ tu/
examples.translation: The rules must be respected by everyone.
examples.note: Modal (doivent) + passive infinitive. The participle agrees with 'règles' (feminine plural) even though it is in the infinitive.

examples.original: En étant informé, tu pourras décider.
examples.phonetic: /ɑ̃ e.tɑ̃ ɛ̃.fɔʁ.me ty pu.ʁa de.si.de/
examples.translation: Being informed, you will be able to decide.
examples.note: Passive gerund: 'en étant' + participle. Used to express condition or cause.

examples.original: Elle voudrait être invitée à la fête.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl vu.dʁɛ ɛtʁ ɛ̃.vi.te a la fɛt/
examples.translation: She would like to be invited to the party.
examples.note: Passive infinitive after a conditional modal. Agreement: 'invitée' (feminine singular because of 'elle').

title: Estilo indirecto avanzado (concordance des temps)
bridge: In Spanish, when we switch to indirect speech, verb tenses adapt similarly to French, but there are key differences in tense concordance and in the use of the subjunctive. For example, in Spanish we say 'Dijo que vendría' (simple conditional) while in French we use 'Il a dit qu'il viendrait' (conditionnel présent), but in French the concordance is stricter and the pluperfect subjunctive is practically nonexistent. Additionally, in French, indirect questions require 'si' (without accent) for yes/no questions, and subject inversion is lost in the indirect form. Pay attention to tense changes: passé composé becomes plus-que-parfait, imparfait remains, and future becomes conditionnel.
rule:
In French, when switching to indirect speech in the past, verb tenses undergo a systematic transformation:

1. **Present → Imparfait**: 'Il dit : « Je mange »' → 'Il a dit qu'il mangeait.'
2. **Passé composé → Plus-que-parfait**: 'Il a dit : « J'ai mangé »' → 'Il a dit qu'il avait mangé.'
3. **Futur simple → Conditionnel présent**: 'Il dira : « Je mangerai »' → 'Il a dit qu'il mangerait.'
4. **Futur antérieur → Conditionnel passé**: 'Il a dit : « J'aurai mangé »' → 'Il a dit qu'il aurait mangé.'

When the introductory verb is in the present, the tense stays the same: 'Il dit qu'il mange.'

**Exceptions and particularities:**
- The subjunctive is maintained in indirect speech, but the tense may change: 'subjonctif présent' to 'subjonctif imparfait' (although the latter is formal and almost only literary).
- Time and place expressions change: 'aujourd'hui' → 'ce jour-là', 'hier' → 'la veille', 'demain' → 'le lendemain', 'ici' → 'là-bas'.
- Total indirect questions are introduced with 'si' (without accent), and no inversion is used: 'Il demande : « Viens-tu ? »' → 'Il demande si tu viens.'
- Imperatives are transformed into infinitives preceded by 'de': 'Il a dit : « Viens ! »' → 'Il a dit de venir.'
- Free indirect speech in narrative (without introductory verbs) is common in literature, but not in conversation.

concept_examples.text: Il a dit qu'il avait fini son travail.
concept_examples.translation: He said he had finished his work.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il a di kil avɛ fini sɔ̃ travaj/

concept_examples.text: Elle a demandé si nous viendrions à la fête.
concept_examples.translation: She asked if we would come to the party.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɛl a dəmɑ̃de si nu vjɛ̃dʁiɔ̃ a la fɛt/

concept_examples.text: Ils ont affirmé qu'ils partiraient le lendemain.
concept_examples.translation: They affirmed that they would leave the next day.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ilz ɔ̃ afiʁme kil paʁtiʁɛ lə lɑ̃dmɛ̃/

concept_examples.text: Il m'a dit de lui téléphoner dès que possible.
concept_examples.translation: He told me to call him as soon as possible.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il ma di də lɥi telefɔne dɛ kə pɔsibl/

common_error.wrong: Il a dit qu'il va à Paris. (cuando el verbo introductor está en pasado y la acción es pasada)
common_error.correct: Il a dit qu'il allait à Paris.
common_error.correct_alt: Il a dit qu'il irait à Paris. (si es futuro respecto al pasado)
common_error.explanation: The error occurs because, in Spanish, we often say 'dijo que va a París' mixing tenses, and it is assumed that French is the same. However, in French, if the introductory verb is in the past, the present of the subordinate clause must become imparfait (allait), and the conditional (irait) if the action is subsequent. The present is not maintained as in Spanish. To avoid this error, always check the tense of the introductory verb and apply the concordance: past → imparfait, plus-que-parfait, or conditionnel.

examples.original: Il a dit : « Je vais bien » → Il a dit qu'il allait bien.
examples.phonetic: /il a di kil alɛ bjɛ̃/
examples.translation: He said: 'I am well' → He said that he was well.
examples.note: Notice how the present 'vais' becomes imparfait 'allait' after an introductory verb in the past.

examples.original: Elle a raconté : « J'ai vu un film » → Elle a raconté qu'elle avait vu un film.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl a aʁakɔ̃te kɛl avɛ vy œ̃ film/
examples.translation: She recounted: 'I saw a film' → She recounted that she had seen a film.
examples.note: The passé composé 'ai vu' becomes plus-que-parfait 'avait vu'.

examples.original: Ils ont promis : « Nous reviendrons » → Ils ont promis qu'ils reviendraient.
examples.phonetic: /ilz ɔ̃ pʁɔmi kil ʁəvjɛ̃dʁɛ/
examples.translation: They promised: 'We will return' → They promised that they would return.
examples.note: The future 'reviendrons' becomes conditional 'reviendraient'.

examples.original: Il demande : « Où vas-tu ? » → Il demande où tu vas.
examples.phonetic: /il dəmɑ̃d u ty va/
examples.translation: He asks: 'Where are you going?' → He asks where you are going.
examples.note: In indirect questions, there is no subject inversion, and the word order is normal.

examples.original: Elle a demandé : « Est-ce que tu viens ? » → Elle a demandé si tu venais.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl a dəmɑ̃de si ty vənɛ/
examples.translation: She asked: 'Are you coming?' → She asked if you were coming.
examples.note: Note the change from 'est-ce que' to 'si' and the tense concordance (present 'viens' to imperfect 'venais').

examples.original: Il m'a demandé : « Qu'est-ce que vous avez décidé ? » → Il m'a demandé ce que nous avions décidé.
examples.phonetic: /il ma dəmɑ̃de sə kə nu avjɔ̃ deside/
examples.translation: He asked me: 'What have you decided?' → He asked me what we had decided.
examples.note: For questions with 'qu'est-ce que', 'ce que' is used in the indirect form, and the tense changes to plus-que-parfait.

examples.original: Il m'a ordonné : « Ferme la porte ! » → Il m'a ordonné de fermer la porte.
examples.phonetic: /il ma ɔʁdɔne də fɛʁme la pɔʁt/
examples.translation: He ordered me: 'Close the door!' → He ordered me to close the door.
examples.note: Imperatives become infinitives preceded by 'de'.

examples.original: Elle a dit : « Je ferai ça demain » → Elle a dit qu'elle ferait ça le lendemain.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl a di k‿ɛl fəʁɛ sa lə lɑ̃dmɛ̃/
examples.translation: She said: 'I will do it tomorrow' → She said she would do it the next day.
examples.note: The pronoun 'demain' changes to 'le lendemain', and the future 'ferai' to conditional 'ferait'.

examples.original: Il a avoué : « J'avais menti » → Il a avoué qu'il avait menti.
examples.phonetic: /il a avwe kil avɛ mɑ̃ti/
examples.translation: He confessed: 'I had lied' → He confessed that he had lied.
examples.note: The plus-que-parfait remains the same in indirect speech, as there is no additional transformation.

title: Inversion for emphasis / Inversión para énfasis (Not only..., Rarely...)
bridge: In Spanish, to emphasize we use structures like 'No solo... sino también...' or 'Rara vez...' without inverting the subject-verb order. In French, when certain adverbs or negative expressions (rarement, à peine, non seulement, jamais, etc.) are placed at the beginning of the sentence, an inversion of the subject and verb occurs, similar to questions. This inversion is obligatory in formal register and optional in informal, but it is a distinctive feature of French that does not exist in Spanish, where the adverb is simply placed before without changing the order. Note: the inversion only occurs if the adverb is at the beginning; if it goes after the verb, there is no inversion.
rule: In French, when certain adverbs or phrases of frequency or emphasis are placed in initial position, the subject and verb (or subject and auxiliary verb if compound tense) must be inverted. This construction is typical of a careful (soutenu) register and is used for emphasis. The adverbs and phrases that trigger it include: rarement (rarely), à peine (hardly), non seulement (not only), jamais (never), encore (still/yet), aussi (also, in a consecutive sense), sans doute (without doubt), en vain (in vain), entre autres. The inversion is simple: if the subject is a pronoun, it is placed after the verb and joined with a hyphen: Rarement a-t-il fait si chaud. If the subject is a noun or a non-personal pronoun, a personal repetition pronoun (il/elle/ils/elles) is added after the verb: À peine Marie est-elle arrivée. In compound tenses, the subject is placed between the auxiliary verb and the participle: Non seulement il a fini, mais... → Non seulement a-t-il fini, mais... This inversion is also used to avoid repetition in links (aussi, en effet). It is important not to confuse it with interrogative inversion; here the intonation is affirmative and there is no question mark. In informal register, inversion can be avoided by placing the adverb after the verb: Il a rarement fait si chaud. However, in formal texts, this inversion is the norm.

concept_examples.text: Non seulement il parle français, mais il parle aussi espagnol.
concept_examples.translation: Not only does he speak French, but he also speaks Spanish.
concept_examples.phonetic: /nɔ̃ sœl.mɑ̃ il paʁl fʁɑ̃.sɛ, mɛ il paʁl o.si ɛs.pa.ɲɔl/

concept_examples.text: Rarement a-t-on vu un tel succès.
concept_examples.translation: Rarely has such success been seen.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʁa.ʁə.mɑ̃ a.tɔ̃ vy œ̃ tɛl syk.sɛ/

concept_examples.text: À peine était-elle arrivée que le téléphone a sonné.
concept_examples.translation: Hardly had she arrived when the phone rang.
concept_examples.phonetic: /a pɛn e.tɛ.tɛl a.ʁi.ve kə lə te.le.fɔn a sɔ.ne/

concept_examples.text: En vain avons-nous cherché la solution.
concept_examples.translation: In vain did we search for the solution.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɑ̃ vɛ̃ a.vɔ.nu ʃɛʁ.ʃe la sɔ.ly.sjɔ̃/

common_error.wrong: Non seulement il a fini, mais il est parti.
common_error.correct: Non seulement a-t-il fini, mais il est parti.
common_error.correct_alt: Non seulement il a fini, mais il est aussi parti.
common_error.explanation: The typical error is keeping the subject-verb order after 'non seulement' at the beginning of the sentence, because in Spanish we say 'No solo terminó, sino que se fue' with normal order. In French, the presence of 'non seulement' in initial position requires the inversion of the subject and the auxiliary verb. To avoid it, remember that negative or restrictive expressions like 'non seulement', 'rarement', 'à peine' at the beginning of the sentence force inversion. If in doubt, you can place the expression after the verb (il a non seulement fini...), but it is less emphatic.

levels.label: Introduction aux inversions après les adverbes

examples.original: Rarement ai-je vu une telle beauté.
examples.phonetic: /ʁa.ʁə.mɑ̃ ɛʒ vy yn tɛl bo.te/
examples.translation: Rarely have I seen such beauty.
examples.note: Notice the inversion of the subject pronoun 'je' after the adverb 'rarement'.

examples.original: À peine a-t-il commencé à pleuvoir.
examples.phonetic: /a pɛn a.til kɔ.mɑ̃.se a plø.vwaʁ/
examples.translation: Hardly had it begun to rain.
examples.note: The pronoun 'il' is inverted with the auxiliary verb 'a'; a euphonic 't' is added for pronunciation.

examples.original: Jamais je n'ai vu un tel film.
examples.phonetic: /ʒa.mɛ ʒə nɛ vy œ̃ tɛl film/
examples.translation: I have never seen such a film.
examples.note: This is the informal form without inversion; in formal register it would be 'Jamais n'ai-je vu...'.

examples.original: Non seulement elle est intelligente, mais aussi charmante.
examples.phonetic: /nɔ̃ sœl.mɑ̃ ɛl ɛt ɛ̃.te.li.ʒɑ̃t, mɛ o.si ʃaʁ.mɑ̃t/
examples.translation: Not only is she intelligent, but also charming.
examples.note: When 'non seulement' is at the beginning, the subject 'elle' is inverted: 'est-elle'.

examples.original: Aussi a-t-il décidé de partir.
examples.phonetic: /o.si a.til de.si.de də paʁ.tiʁ/
examples.translation: Therefore he decided to leave.
examples.note: Here 'aussi' means 'therefore' and requires inversion; do not confuse with 'aussi' = also, which does not require it.

examples.original: Il a non seulement perdu, mais aussi gagné.
examples.phonetic: /il a nɔ̃ sœl.mɑ̃ pɛʁ.dy, mɛ o.si ɡa.ne/
examples.translation: He has not only lost, but also won.
examples.note: If 'non seulement' goes after the verb, there is no inversion. Inversion only occurs at the beginning.

levels.label: Inversion avec noms et sujets complexes
levels.translation: Inversion with nouns and complex subjects

examples.original: À peine les enfants sont-ils rentrés que la pluie a commencé.
examples.phonetic: /a pɛn le zɑ̃.fɑ̃ sɔ̃.til ʁɑ̃.tʁe kə la plɥi a kɔ.mɑ̃.se/
examples.translation: Hardly had the children come in when it started to rain.
examples.note: With a noun subject 'les enfants', the pronoun 'ils' is added after the verb: 'sont-ils'.

examples.original: Rarement une telle occasion se présente-t-elle.
examples.phonetic: /ʁa.ʁə.mɑ̃ yn tɛl o.ka.zjɔ̃ sə pʁe.zɑ̃t.tɛl/
examples.translation: Rarely does such an occasion present itself.
examples.note: The subject 'une telle occasion' is feminine singular; 'elle' is used for the inversion.

examples.original: En vain les parents ont-ils cherché leur fils.
examples.phonetic: /ɑ̃ vɛ̃ le pa.ʁɑ̃ ɔ̃.til ʃɛʁ.ʃe lœʁ fis/
examples.translation: In vain did the parents search for their son.
examples.note: 'ils' is added after the auxiliary verb 'ont' to agree with 'les parents'.

examples.original: Non seulement les étudiants sont-ils fatigués, mais aussi démotivés.
examples.phonetic: /nɔ̃ sœl.mɑ̃ lez‿e.ty.djɑ̃ sɔ̃.til fa.ti.ɡe, mɛ o.si de.mɔ.ti.ve/
examples.translation: Not only are the students tired, but also demotivated.
examples.note: The inversion is done with 'ils' because the subject is 'les étudiants'.

title: Les constructions clivées (C'est ... qui/que) / Cleft constructions (It is ... who/that)
bridge: In Spanish, we use structures like 'Fue Juan quien lo dijo' or 'Es ahora cuando hay que actuar' to emphasize an element. In French, the equivalent construction is 'C'est ... qui/que', but there are key differences: the verb in the subordinate clause agrees with the pronoun 'qui' (not with 'c'est'), and 'que' is used for objects. Additionally, in French the relative pronoun is not omitted as sometimes happens in Spanish ('Es Juan quien lo dijo' → 'C'est Jean qui l'a dit', but 'Fue en París que nos conocimos' does not allow 'donde' in colloquial French). Be careful not to use 'ce qui/ce que' instead of 'qui/que' when the antecedent is clear.
rule:
In French, the cleft construction allows highlighting an element of the sentence (subject, object, adverbial, etc.) using the structure 'C'est/ce sont + [element] + relative pronoun (qui/que/dont/où) + [rest]'.

1. **Emphasizing the subject**: Use 'qui' as the relative pronoun, and the verb of the subordinate clause agrees with the emphasized noun/pronoun.
   - Ex: 'C'est moi qui ai téléphoné.' (It is I who called).
   - If the subject is plural, use 'ce sont' (more formal) or 'c'est' (colloquial) + verb in plural.

2. **Emphasizing the direct or indirect object**: Use 'que' as the relative pronoun (not 'qui').
   - Ex: 'C'est ce que je veux.' (It is what I want).

3. **With prepositions**: 'C'est ... que' is used for prepositional complements (place, time, manner).
   - Ex: 'C'est à Paris que j'habite.' (It is in Paris that I live).
   - 'C'est en 2020 que je suis arrivé.' (It was in 2020 that I arrived).

4. **Special forms**: With 'dont' for complements of verbs with 'de', and 'où' for place/time.

**Exceptions and colloquial uses**: In spoken French, 'c'est' is frequently used instead of 'ce sont' (e.g., 'C'est eux qui...'), but in formal register 'ce sont' is preferred. Additionally, 'c'est ... qui' is not used to emphasize a verb (use 'ce que ... c'est'), and in negation it is written 'ce n'est pas ... qui/que'. Agreement with 'qui' is mandatory: 'C'est nous qui sommes responsables' (not 'sommes'? Yes, we are).

concept_examples.translation: It is Jean who won the prize.
concept_examples.phonetic: /sɛ ʒɑ̃ ki a ɡaɲe lə pʁi/

concept_examples.text: C'est la liberté que nous cherchons.
concept_examples.translation: It is freedom that we seek.
concept_examples.phonetic: /sɛ la libɛʁte kə nu ʃɛʁʃɔ̃/

concept_examples.text: C'est à Paris que je voudrais vivre.
concept_examples.translation: It is in Paris that I would like to live.
concept_examples.phonetic: /sɛ a paʁi kə ʒə vudʁɛ vivʁ/

concept_examples.text: Ce dont je parle, c'est ta décision.
concept_examples.translation: What I am talking about is your decision.
concept_examples.phonetic: /sə dɔ̃ ʒə paʁl sɛ ta desizjɔ̃/

common_error.explanation: The classic error is not agreeing the verb of the subordinate clause with the antecedent (in this case 'moi'). In Spanish we also agree ('soy yo quien ha llamado' vs 'soy yo quien he llamado' – although in Spanish both are accepted, in French only agreement with the emphasized pronoun is correct). Therefore, you must conjugate the verb according to 'moi', 'toi', 'nous', 'eux', etc.

levels.label: C'est ... qui pour le sujet
levels.translation: It is ... who for the subject

examples.original: C'est Marie qui chante le mieux.
examples.phonetic: /sɛ maʁi ki ʃɑ̃t lə mjø/
examples.translation: It is Marie who sings best.
examples.note: The verb 'chante' agrees with 'Marie' (3rd singular), not with 'c'est'.

examples.original: C'est nous qui organisons la fête.
examples.phonetic: /sɛ nu ki ɔʁɡanizɔ̃ la fɛt/

examples.note: Although 'c'est' is singular, the verb 'organisons' is conjugated in 1st plural because of 'nous'.

levels.label: C'est ... que pour l'objet ou le complément
levels.translation: It is ... that for the object or complement

examples.original: C'est le rapport que je dois finir.
examples.phonetic: /sɛ lə ʁapɔʁ kə ʒə dwa finiʁ/
examples.translation: It is the report that I must finish.
examples.note: We use 'que' because 'rapport' is the direct object of the verb 'finir'.

examples.original: C'est avec plaisir que j'accepte.
examples.phonetic: /sɛ avɛk pleziʁ kə ʒaksɛpt/
examples.translation: It is with pleasure that I accept.
examples.note: For complements of manner or accompaniment, 'que' is used, not 'dont'.

levels.label: C'est ... dont/où et constructions impositives
levels.translation: It is ... of whom/where and emphatic constructions with verbs

examples.original: C'est de toi dont je parle.
examples.phonetic: /sɛ də twa dɔ̃ ʒə paʁl/
examples.translation: It is of you that I speak.
examples.note: When the verb governs 'de', we use 'dont'. Do not confuse with 'que'.

examples.original: C'est là où je me sens chez moi.
examples.phonetic: /sɛ la u ʒə mə sɑ̃ ʃe mwa/
examples.translation: It is there where I feel at home.
examples.note: 'où' is used for place, but in formal register sometimes 'que' is preferred (C'est là que...).

examples.original: Ce que je veux, c'est partir en vacances.
examples.phonetic: /sə kə ʒə vø sɛ paʁtiʁ ɑ̃ vakɑ̃s/
examples.translation: What I want is to go on vacation.
examples.note: To emphasize a verb or an action, the structure 'ce que ... c'est' is used. Here 'qui' is not used.

title: La nominalisation / Nominalization
bridge: In Spanish, we often use infinitives or phrases with 'el hecho de' to nominalize, but in French it is very common to use suffixes like -tion, -ment, -ure, -ité, -ance. For example, 'la transformación' (transformer) in French is the same as in Spanish, but be careful with false friends: 'demander' gives 'demande' (request), not 'demanda' as in Spanish. Furthermore, French uses nominalizations more often than Spanish in formal contexts, so mastering them is key for a B2 level.
rule: Nominalization consists of converting a verb or an adjective into a noun. In French, the most frequent suffixes are: -tion/-sion (for verbs in -er, -ir, -re: informer→information, décider→décision), -ment (for verbs in -er: changement, gouvernement), -ure (for verbs in -re: ouverture, fermeture), -ance/-ence (for verbs and adjectives: naissance, patience), -ité (for adjectives: rapidité, beauté), -esse (for adjectives: tendresse), -age (for actions: lavage). There are also nominalizations without a suffix (le rire from rire, le travail from travailler). The gender of the resulting noun is generally feminine with -tion/-sion, -ure, -ance, -ité, and masculine with -ment, -age, -oir. Exceptions: 'courrier' (from courir) is masculine, and 'visite' (from visiter) is feminine. For B2, it is important to use nominalizations in formal registers, in academic and professional writing, and to replace verbal constructions for greater conciseness. Also note that some nominalizations change the spelling of the root (découvrir→découverte, s'asseoir→assise).

concept_examples.text: Son ouverture d'esprit est remarquable.

concept_examples.phonetic: /sɔ̃.n‿u.vɛʁ.tyʁ d‿ɛs.pʁi ɛ ʁə.maʁ.kabl/

concept_examples.text: La beauté de ce paysage m'a émerveillé.

common_error.wrong: La décision de partir a été difficile à prendre.
common_error.correct: Prendre la décision de partir a été difficile.
common_error.correct_alt: La décision de partir a été difficile à prendre.
common_error.explanation: This example is actually correct. A typical mistake for Spanish speakers is using 'la demande' for 'demanda' in the sense of 'legal demand' or 'job demand'. In French, 'la demande' is 'request' or 'application'. For 'demanda' in the economic or legal sense, 'la demande' is also used, but in the legal field 'demande' is correct. Another common mistake is confusing 'le changement' with 'el cambio' when in Spanish 'cambio' is used as currency, but in French that is 'la monnaie'. To avoid errors, learn nominalizations as vocabulary, not as automatic rules, and verify with a dictionary.

examples.original: La liberté est un droit fondamental.
examples.phonetic: /la li.bɛʁ.te ɛt‿œ̃ dʁwa fɔ̃.da.mɑ̃.tal/

examples.note: -té (like -dad) for adjectives in -eux, -if, etc. 'Libre' → 'liberté'.

examples.original: Sa gentillesse a conquis tout le monde.
examples.phonetic: /sa ʒɑ̃.ti.jɛs a kɔ̃.ki tu lə mɔ̃d/
examples.translation: His kindness won everyone over.

levels.label: Nominalisation sans suffixe et cas particuliers
levels.translation: Nominalization without suffix and special cases

examples.note: Sometimes the infinitive becomes a noun directly: 'rire' (verb) → 'le rire' (noun).

examples.translation: We enjoyed the visit to the museum.
examples.note: Here 'visite' comes from 'visiter', the spelling changes and the gender is feminine, unlike 'visita' in Spanish.

examples.original: L'ouverture des magasins est à neuf heures.

title: Modales compuestos: aurait dû, aurait pu, devait avoir / Compound modals: should have, could have, must have had
bridge: In French, compound modals express unfulfilled past conditions, regrets, or past deductions. The structure for regret or hypothetical past possibility is 'auxiliary conditional + modal participle + infinitive' (e.g., 'j'aurais dû' = I should have, 'j'aurais pu' = I could have). However, watch out for 'devait avoir' (imperfect of devoir + infinitive), which expresses a past deduction or probability ('must have had / was supposed to have') rather than regret. Pay attention to subject-participle agreement when using 'être' as the auxiliary.
rule:
Advanced modals in French are formed with the past conditional (conditionnel passé) of the modal verb + infinitive of the main verb. The main forms are:
1. **Avoir dû + infinitive** (should have): 'j'aurais dû' (I should have).
2. **Avoir pu + infinitive** (could have): 'j'aurais pu' (I could have).
3. **Devoir + infinitive in the imperfect** (past obligation/deduction): 'je devais' (imperfect) or 'j'ai dû' (passé composé).
4. **Avoir voulu + infinitive** (would have liked to): 'j'aurais voulu'.
Uses:
- Unfulfilled past hypotheticals: 'Si j'avais su, j'aurais agi autrement' (If I had known, I would have acted differently).
- Regrets or reproaches: 'Il aurait dû venir' (He should have come).
- With 'être' as the main auxiliary, the past participle agrees with the subject: 'elle serait allée' (she would have gone).
- In negation, 'ne' precedes the auxiliary and 'pas' follows the participle: 'je n'aurais pas dû' (I shouldn't have).
- The form 'devait + infinitive' (imperfect of devoir) is used for past deductions or expected actions: 'Il devait avoir 20 ans' (He must have been 20 years old).
Exceptions: with pronominal verbs, 'être' is used as the auxiliary: 'je me serais trompé' (I would have been mistaken). In informal spoken French, 'ne' is often dropped in negation.

concept_examples.text: J'aurais dû étudier plus pour l'examen.
concept_examples.translation: I should have studied more for the exam.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʒ‿ɔʁɛ dy etɥidje ply puʁ lɛɡzam/

concept_examples.text: Elle aurait pu venir nous voir hier.
concept_examples.translation: She could have come to see us yesterday.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɛl ɔʁɛ py vənir nu vwaʁ jɛʁ/

concept_examples.text: Nous aurions voulu vous accompagner.
concept_examples.translation: We would have liked to accompany you.
concept_examples.phonetic: /nu z‿ɔʁjɔ̃ vuly vu zakɔ̃paɲe/

concept_examples.text: Tu devais avoir raison.
concept_examples.translation: You must have been right.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ty dəvɛ avwaʁ ʁɛzɔ̃/

common_error.explanation: This error occurs when trying to translate a past regret using the imperfect 'je devais'. In French, to express regret or a reproach regarding an unperformed past action, you must use the past conditional 'aurait dû' + infinitive. 'Je devais' indicates a past obligation ('I was supposed to') or deduction, not regret. Associate 'should have' with the past conditional ('aurais dû').

examples.original: J'aurais dû t'écouter.
examples.phonetic: /ʒ‿ɔʁɛ dy t‿ekute/
examples.translation: I should have listened to you.
examples.note: Used to express regret about a past action. Note that 'avoir dû' is the past conditional of 'devoir'.

examples.original: Tu aurais dû me prévenir.
examples.phonetic: /ty ɔʁɛ dy mə pʁevniʁ/
examples.translation: You should have warned me.

examples.original: On aurait dû partir plus tôt.

examples.translation: We should have left earlier.
examples.note: Note the agreement: 'partir' is intransitive, but with 'avoir' there is no participle agreement.

levels.label: L'hypothèse et la possibilité (aurait pu, aurait voulu)
levels.translation: Hypothesis and possibility (could have, would have liked to)

examples.phonetic: /il ɔʁɛ py ʁeysiʁ sil‿avɛ ete sɛje/
examples.translation: He could have succeeded if he had tried.
examples.note: Here 'aurait pu' expresses an unfulfilled past capability.

examples.original: Nous aurions voulu visiter le musée, mais il était fermé.
examples.phonetic: /nu z‿ɔʁjɔ̃ vuly vizite lə myze, mɛ il‿ɛtɛ fɛʁme/
examples.translation: We would have liked to visit the museum, but it was closed.
examples.note: 'Aurais voulu' indicates an unfulfilled desire.

examples.original: Elle aurait pu être plus claire.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl ɔʁɛ py ɛtʁ ply klɛʁ/
examples.translation: She could have been clearer.
examples.note: With 'être' as the main verb, 'aurait pu' does not require agreement of the participle 'pu', but the adjective 'claire' agrees with the subject 'elle'.

examples.original: Il devait avoir faim après ce long voyage.
examples.phonetic: /il dəvɛ avwaʁ fɛ̃ apʁi sə lɔ̃ vwajaʒ/
examples.translation: He must have been hungry after that long journey.
examples.note: 'Devait' (imperfect) is used for deductions in the past, not the conditional.

examples.original: Elle devait être très fatiguée.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl dəvɛ ɛtʁ tʁɛ fatige/
examples.translation: She must have been very tired.
examples.note: 'devait être' expresses a probability or assumption in the past.

examples.original: Ils devaient avoir raison.
examples.phonetic: /il dəvɛ avwaʁ ʁɛzɔ̃/
examples.translation: They must have been right.
examples.note: Do not confuse with 'ils auraient dû' (they should have).

title: Les participes présents et les clauses de participe (Caminando por la calle, vi...)
bridge: In Spanish, we use the gerund (-ando/-iendo) to express simultaneous or causal actions: 'Caminando por la calle, vi a un amigo'. In French, there is an equivalent: the participe présent (en marchant) and the gérondif (en marchant). Unlike Spanish, French distinguishes between the simple present participle (marchant) and the compound form (ayant marché), and the gérondif always takes the preposition 'en'. Moreover, in French, the present participle agrees only when used as an adjective, not in verbal constructions. The typical error is omitting the preposition 'en' or using the present participle where the gérondif is required.
rule: In French, the participe présent is formed from the stem of the first‑person plural of the present indicative (nous) + -ant (e.g., nous parlons → parlant). The gérondif is built with 'en' + participe présent (en parlant). It is used to express: 1) a simultaneous action: 'Il regarde la télé en mangeant' (He watches TV while eating). 2) a causal or conditional relationship: 'En travaillant dur, tu réussiras' (Working hard, you will succeed). The present participle without 'en' (called participe présent) is used as a verb in subordinate clauses: 'Ayant fini ses devoirs, il est sorti' (Having finished his homework, he went out), or as a verbal adjective agreeing in gender and number: 'des histoires passionnantes' (exciting stories). Exceptions: the verbs être (étant), avoir (ayant), savoir (sachant), and some verbs with irregular stems (aller → allant, venir → venant). Unlike Spanish, the French gerund does not change according to the subject, and its position is more flexible. At B2 level, you are expected to use these constructions to enrich your sentences and avoid repetitions.

concept_examples.text: En marchant dans la rue, j'ai vu un ami.
concept_examples.translation: Walking down the street, I saw a friend.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɑ̃ maʁ.ʃɑ̃ dɑ̃ la ʁy, ʒ‿e vy œ̃n‿ami/

concept_examples.text: Ayant terminé ses devoirs, elle est sortie.
concept_examples.translation: Having finished her homework, she went out.
concept_examples.phonetic: /e.jɑ̃ tɛʁ.mi.ne se də.vwaʁ, ɛl ɛ sɔʁ.ti/

concept_examples.text: En attendant le bus, je lisais un livre.
concept_examples.translation: Waiting for the bus, I was reading a book.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɑ̃ nɑ.tɑ̃ dɑ̃ lə bys, ʒ‿ə li.zɛ œ̃ livʁ/

concept_examples.text: Étant fatigué, il s'est couché tôt.
concept_examples.translation: Being tired, he went to bed early.
concept_examples.phonetic: /e.tɑ̃ fa.ti.ge, il sɛ ku.ʃe to/

common_error.wrong: Marchant dans la rue, j'ai vu un ami.
common_error.correct: En marchant dans la rue, j'ai vu un ami.
common_error.correct_alt: En marchant dans la rue, j'ai vu un ami. (Sin 'en' para simultáneo)
common_error.explanation: The mistake occurs because in Spanish the gerund does not take a preposition ('caminando'). In French, to express simultaneity with the subject, the gérondif with 'en' is required. Without 'en', the present participle (marchant) is used in constructions such as 'Marchant vite, il arrive' (Walking quickly, he arrives), but it is less common and usually implies a causal relationship. To avoid the error, identify whether the action is simultaneous (use 'en') or prior (use 'ayant + past participle').

examples.original: Les enfants jouant dans le parc sont mes voisins.
examples.phonetic: /le z‿ɑ̃.fɑ̃ ʒwɑ̃ dɑ̃ lə paʁk sɔ̃ me vwa.zɛ̃/
examples.translation: The children playing in the park are my neighbours.
examples.note: Here 'jouant' functions as a verbal adjective, agreeing with 'enfants' (masculine plural).

examples.original: Ayant faim, nous avons mangé au restaurant.
examples.phonetic: /e.jɑ̃ fɛ̃, nu z‿a.vɔ̃ mɑ̃.ʒe o ʁɛs.to.ʁɑ̃/
examples.translation: Being hungry, we ate at the restaurant.
examples.note: The compound participle 'ayant' + past participle expresses anteriority.

examples.original: Sachant la vérité, elle a réagi calmement.
examples.phonetic: /sa.ʃɑ̃ la ve.ʁi.te, ɛl a ʁe.a.ʒi kal.mə.mɑ̃/
examples.translation: Knowing the truth, she reacted calmly.
examples.note: Irregular verb: savoir → sachant.

examples.original: Elle chante en prenant sa douche.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl ʃɑ̃t ɑ̃ pʁə.nɑ̃ sa duʃ/
examples.translation: She sings while taking a shower.
examples.note: Simultaneous action: 'en' + present participle.

examples.original: En parlant avec lui, j'ai compris son problème.
examples.phonetic: /ɑ̃ paʁ.lɑ̃ a.vɛk lɥi, ʒ‿e kɔ̃.pʁi sɔ̃ pʁɔ.blɛm/
examples.translation: Speaking with him, I understood his problem.
examples.note: Expresses an action that occurs at the same time as another.

examples.original: En partant tôt, nous éviterons les embouteillages.

examples.translation: Leaving early, we will avoid traffic jams.
examples.note: Conditional use: if you leave early, you will avoid the jams.

examples.original: Il faut manger en buvant de l'eau.
examples.phonetic: /il fo mɑ̃.ʒe ɑ̃ by.vɑ̃ də l‿o/
examples.translation: One must eat while drinking water.
examples.note: The gérondif can also express a manner of doing something.

levels.label: Le participe présent et le gérondif (différences et pièges)
levels.translation: The present participle and the gerund (differences and pitfalls)

examples.original: Étant donné son âge, il a fait un effort.
examples.phonetic: /e.tɑ̃ do.ne sɔ̃ n‿aʒ, il a fɛ œ̃ n‿e.fɔʁ/
examples.translation: Given his age, he made an effort.
examples.note: 'Étant donné' is a fixed causal expression.

examples.original: Il a traversé la rue en courant.
examples.phonetic: /il a tʁa.vɛʁ.se la ʁy ɑ̃ ku.ʁɑ̃/
examples.translation: He crossed the street running.
examples.note: Here 'en courant' indicates manner (how he crossed).

examples.original: Les résultats étant mauvais, nous avons changé de stratégie.
examples.phonetic: /le ʁe.zyl.ta z‿e.tɑ̃ mɔ.vɛ, nu z‿a.vɔ̃ ʃɑ̃.ʒe də stʁa.te.ʒi/
examples.translation: The results being bad, we changed strategy.
examples.note: The present participle with a subject different from that of the main clause (absolute).

examples.original: Ayant travaillé toute la journée, il était épuisé.
examples.phonetic: /e.jɑ̃ tʁa.va.je tut la ʒuʁ.ne, il e.tɛ e.pɥi.ze/
examples.translation: Having worked all day, he was exhausted.
examples.note: Use the compound participle for an action prior in time.

title: Subjonctif formel (il est essentiel qu'il soit...) / Formal Subjunctive (it is essential that he be...)
bridge: In Spanish, the subjunctive is used in a similar way, but in French you have to pay attention to tense agreement and specific forms. For example, in Spanish we say 'es esencial que él sea', but in French we use 'qu'il soit' with the same structure. However, French has forms like 'qu'il fût' in the imperfect subjunctive that are hardly used in spoken language, whereas in Spanish the imperfect subjunctive remains common. Moreover, French often omits the subject pronoun in the impersonal form, and you must take care of the pronunciation of the endings that are silent.
rule: The French subjunctive is used after impersonal expressions such as 'il est essentiel que', 'il est important que', 'il faut que', etc. It is formed with 'que' + the verb in the subjunctive. The present subjunctive endings are: -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent for -er verbs; for -ir and -re verbs, the endings are -isse, -isses, -isse, -issions, -issiez, -issent. Irregular verbs such as 'être' (sois, sois, soit, soyons, soyez, soient) and 'avoir' (aie, aies, ait, ayons, ayez, aient) have their own forms. In formal language, the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., 'qu'il fût') is used in literary contexts, although in spoken practice the present subjunctive is preferred. Exceptions: after certain verbs like 'espérer' the subjunctive is not used, but the indicative. It is also used after conjunctions such as 'avant que', 'pour que', 'bien que'.

concept_examples.text: Il est essentiel qu'il soit présent à la réunion.
concept_examples.translation: It is essential that he be present at the meeting.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il ɛt‿esɑ̃sjɛl kil swa pʁezɑ̃ a la ʁeɥnjɔ̃/

concept_examples.text: Il faut que nous ayons fini avant midi.
concept_examples.translation: It is necessary that we have finished before noon.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il fo kə nu.z‿ɛjɔ̃ fini avɑ̃ midi/

concept_examples.text: Bien qu'il soit fatigué, il continue à travailler.
concept_examples.translation: Even though he is tired, he continues working.
concept_examples.phonetic: /bjɛ̃ kil swa fatige, il kɔ̃tiny a tʁavaje/

concept_examples.text: Il est important que vous sachiez la vérité.
concept_examples.translation: It is important that you (plural) know the truth.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il ɛt‿ɛ̃pɔʁtɑ̃ kə vu saʃje la veʁite/

common_error.wrong: Il est essentiel qu'il est présent à la réunion.
common_error.correct: Il est essentiel qu'il soit présent à la réunion.
common_error.correct_alt: Il est essentiel qu'il soit présent à la réunion.
common_error.explanation: The common mistake is using the indicative 'est' instead of the subjunctive 'soit' after 'il est essentiel que'. In Spanish, the indicative is sometimes used in more colloquial contexts, but in French the subjunctive is mandatory after these impersonal expressions. To avoid it, remember that after 'il est + adjective + que' the subjunctive always follows when it expresses necessity, importance, or feeling.

levels.label: Le subjonctif présent des verbes réguliers
levels.translation: The present subjunctive of regular verbs

examples.original: Il est important que tu parles français chaque jour.
examples.phonetic: /il ɛt‿ɛ̃pɔʁtɑ̃ kə ty paʁl fʁɑ̃sɛ ʃak ʒuʁ/
examples.translation: It is important that you speak French every day.
examples.note: The verb 'parler' in the subjunctive has the same form as the present indicative for 'tu', but it is distinguished by the context and the conjunction 'que'.

examples.original: Il faut que nous finissions nos devoirs.
examples.phonetic: /il fo kə nu finisjɔ̃ no dəvwaʁ/
examples.translation: It is necessary that we finish our homework.
examples.note: Notice the '-issions' ending for second-group verbs like 'finir'.

examples.original: Je veux que vous choisissiez le bon chemin.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə vø kə vu ʃwazisje lə bɔ̃ ʃəmɛ̃/
examples.translation: I want you (plural) to choose the right path.
examples.note: The subjunctive of 'choisir' uses the stem 'choisiss-' + endings.

examples.original: Il est essentiel que tu sois honnête.
examples.phonetic: /il ɛt‿esɑ̃sjɛl kə ty swa ɔnɛt/
examples.translation: It is essential that you be honest.
examples.note: The verb 'être' has a special stem: sois, sois, soit, soyons, soyez, soient.

examples.original: Il est dommage qu'elle n'ait pas pu venir.
examples.phonetic: /il ɛt dɔmaʒ kɛl nɛ pa py vəniʁ/
examples.translation: It is a pity that she could not have come.
examples.note: The verb 'avoir' in the subjunctive: aie, aies, ait, ayons, ayez, aient.

examples.original: Il faut que nous sachions la réponse.
examples.phonetic: /il fo kə nu saʃjɔ̃ la ʁepɔ̃s/
examples.translation: It is necessary that we know the answer.
examples.note: The verb 'savoir' has the subjunctive forms 'sache, saches, sache, sachions, sachiez, sachent'.

levels.label: Le subjonctif après les conjonctions et les structures impersonnelles
levels.translation: The subjunctive after conjunctions and impersonal structures

examples.original: Avant qu'il ne parte, nous devons lui parler.
examples.phonetic: /avɑ̃ kil nə paʁt, nu dəvɔ̃ lɥi paʁle/
examples.translation: Before he leaves, we must speak to him.
examples.note: The conjunction 'avant que' requires the subjunctive, often with the expletive 'ne'.

examples.original: Pour que vous compreniez la leçon, je vais la répéter.
examples.phonetic: /puʁ kə vu kɔ̃pʁənje la ləsɔ̃, ʒə vɛ la ʁepete/
examples.translation: So that you (plural) understand the lesson, I will repeat it.
examples.note: The conjunction 'pour que' always takes the subjunctive, even if the action is future.

examples.original: Il est possible qu'ils soient en retard à cause du trafic.
examples.phonetic: /il ɛt pɔsibl kil swa ɑ̃ ʁətaʁ a koz dy tʁafik/
examples.translation: It is possible that they arrive late because of traffic.
examples.note: The expression 'il est possible que' requires the subjunctive, while 'il est probable que' also demands it.

examples.original: Je doute qu'il fasse beau demain.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə dut kil fas bo dəmɛ̃/
examples.translation: I doubt that the weather will be nice tomorrow.
examples.note: The verb 'douter' (affirmative) requires the subjunctive in the subordinate clause.

title: Futur antérieur et futur continu / Future perfect and future continuous
bridge: In French, the future perfect (futur antérieur) is formed with the auxiliary avoir or être in the simple future plus the past participle, similar to the Spanish compound future (habré comido). However, unlike Spanish, French does not have a specific future continuous form (estaré comiendo); it is expressed with the simple future or with the construction 'être en train de' in the future. Watch out for the agreement of the past participle with être and for the choice of auxiliary.
rule: The future perfect (futur antérieur) is used for actions that will be completed at a future moment, or for assumptions about the past. It is formed: auxiliary (avoir or être) in the simple future + past participle. With être, the past participle agrees in gender and number with the subject. Example: 'Quand tu arriveras, j'aurai fini' (When you arrive, I will have finished). For the future continuous, there is no specific tense; the simple future is used (Je travaillerai) or the structure 'être en train de + infinitive' in the future (Je serai en train de travailler). The future perfect is also used for actions that will occur before another future action, often with conjunctions such as 'dès que', 'quand', 'après que'. With 'après que', the verb in the subordinate clause is in the indicative (not the subjunctive as sometimes thought).

concept_examples.text: D'ici demain, j'aurai fini ce rapport.
concept_examples.translation: By tomorrow I will have finished this report.
concept_examples.phonetic: /disi dəmɛ̃, ʒ‿oʁe fini sə ʁapɔʁ/

concept_examples.text: Quand tu reviendras, Marie sera partie depuis une heure.
concept_examples.translation: When you return, Marie will have left for an hour.
concept_examples.phonetic: /kɑ̃ ty ʁəvjɛ̃dʁa, maʁi səʁa paʁti dəpɥi yn œʁ/

concept_examples.text: À cette heure-là, nous serons en train de dîner au restaurant.
concept_examples.translation: At that hour we will be having dinner at the restaurant.
concept_examples.phonetic: /a sɛt œʁ la, nu səʁɔ̃ ɑ̃ tʁɛ̃ də dine o ʁɛstɔʁɑ̃/

concept_examples.text: Elle aura probablement oublié nos rendez-vous.
concept_examples.translation: She will probably have forgotten our appointments.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɛl ɔʁa pʁɔbabləmɑ̃ ublije no ʁɑ̃devu/

common_error.wrong: Quand tu arriveras, j'aurai fini mon travaille.
common_error.correct: Quand tu arriveras, j'aurai fini mon travail.
common_error.correct_alt: Quand tu arriveras, j'aurai terminé mon travail.
common_error.explanation: The error is the spelling of 'travail' (singular). Many students add a final 'e' by analogy with the Spanish 'trabajo'. In French, the singular is 'travail' and the plural is 'travaux'. Pay attention to the spelling of nouns, not just verb conjugation.

examples.original: D'ici lundi, ils auront terminé le projet.
examples.phonetic: /disi lœ̃di, il‿ɔʁɔ̃ tɛʁmine lə pʁɔʒɛ/
examples.translation: By Monday, they will have finished the project.
examples.note: Most verbs use 'avoir' in the future perfect. The past participle does not agree with the subject when 'avoir' is used.

examples.original: Nous aurons déjà mangé quand vous arriverez.
examples.phonetic: /nu‿ɔʁɔ̃ deʒa mɑ̃ʒe kɑ̃ vu‿aʁivʁe/
examples.translation: We will already have eaten when you all arrive.
examples.note: The adverb 'déjà' is placed between the auxiliary and the past participle.

levels.label: Futur antérieur avec être et accord
levels.translation: Future perfect with être and agreement

examples.original: Elle sera partie avant midi.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl səʁa paʁti avɑ̃ midi/
examples.translation: She will have left before noon.
examples.note: With the auxiliary 'être', the past participle agrees in gender and number with the subject.

examples.original: Quand nous serons arrivés, le film aura commencé.
examples.phonetic: /kɑ̃ nu səʁɔ̃ aʁive, lə film ɔʁa kɔmɑ̃se/
examples.translation: When we have arrived, the film will have started.
examples.note: Movement verbs like 'arriver' use 'être'. Here 'serons arrivés' agrees with 'nous' (masculine plural).

levels.label: Futur continu : 'être en train de' et expressions
levels.translation: Future continuous: 'être en train de' and expressions

examples.original: À dix heures, je serai en train de travailler.
examples.phonetic: /a diz‿œʁ, ʒə səʁe ɑ̃ tʁɛ̃ də tʁavaje/
examples.translation: At ten o'clock, I will be working.
examples.note: The construction 'être en train de + infinitive' in the future expresses an ongoing action, similar to the Spanish future continuous.

examples.original: Nous serons en train de faire nos valises quand vous téléphonerez.
examples.phonetic: /nu səʁɔ̃ ɑ̃ tʁɛ̃ də fɛʁ no valiz kɑ̃ vu telefonʁe/
examples.translation: We will be making the suitcases when you call.
examples.note: The simple future of the auxiliary 'être' is used followed by 'en train de' to indicate an ongoing action in the future.

title: Marqueurs du discours / Discourse markers
bridge: In Spanish, discourse markers such as 'however', 'therefore' and 'also' are essential for linking ideas. In French, these connectors serve a similar function, but they present register and placement nuances that differ from Spanish. For example, 'cependant' (however) usually appears at the beginning of the sentence, whereas 'pourtant' (however, but) often comes after the verb. Moreover, some French markers, like 'en effet' (indeed), are used to confirm an idea, while in Spanish 'en efecto' is more formal. One must be careful with false friends: 'actuellement' means 'currently' in the sense of 'at this moment', but 'en réalité' is 'in reality'.
rule: French discourse markers are classified according to their function: addition (et, de plus, en outre), opposition (mais, cependant, pourtant, en revanche), cause (car, parce que, puisque), consequence (donc, ainsi, par conséquent), and discourse organization (d'abord, ensuite, enfin). For a B2 level, it is important to differentiate between registers: 'cependant' is more formal, 'pourtant' is more everyday; 'en revanche' is used to contrast two elements in a more nuanced way than 'mais'. Placement varies: connectors such as 'cependant' and 'pourtant' can appear at the beginning of the sentence, but if they come after the verb, they are used without a comma. 'Car' introduces an explanation and is more formal than 'parce que'. 'Donc' can be placed at the beginning or in the middle, but in spoken language it is often placed at the end as a filler. One must also observe temporal agreement: some connectors like 'puisque' (since) imply a known cause, whereas 'parce que' introduces a new cause. In formal writing, connectors such as 'en effet', 'par conséquent' and 'néanmoins' are preferred.

concept_examples.text: Il pleut, cependant nous irons nous promener.
concept_examples.translation: It rains, however we will go for a walk.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il plø səpɑ̃dɑ̃ nu iʁɔ̃ nu pʁɔmne/

concept_examples.text: Elle a réussi son examen, en effet elle a beaucoup travaillé.
concept_examples.translation: She passed her exam, indeed she worked a lot.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɛl a ʁeysi sɔ̃n ɛgzamɛ̃ ɑ̃nɛfɛt ɛl a boku tʁavaje/

concept_examples.text: Je n'aime pas le café, par contre j'adore le thé.
concept_examples.translation: I don't like coffee, on the other hand I love tea.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʒə nɛm pɑ lə kafe paʁ kɔ̃tʁ ʒadɔʁ lə te/

concept_examples.text: Il faut partir tôt, sinon nous serons en retard.
concept_examples.translation: We must leave early, if not we will be late.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il fo paʁtiʁ to sinɔ̃ nu səʁɔ̃ ɑ̃ ʁətaʁ/

common_error.wrong: Je suis fatigué, cependant je vais continuer.
common_error.correct: Je suis fatigué, pourtant je vais continuer.
common_error.correct_alt: Je suis fatigué, néanmoins je vais continuer.
common_error.explanation: In Spanish, 'however' is used both for logical contrast and for concession. In French, 'cependant' is more formal and often placed at the beginning or after a verb, but in everyday language 'pourtant' is preferred to express a concession (despite something). 'Néanmoins' is even more formal and also correct. The error arises because learners directly transfer the Spanish use of 'however' without considering register and placement. To avoid this mistake, think about the context: if it is an informal conversation, use 'pourtant'; if it is an academic text, 'cependant' or 'néanmoins' are appropriate.

examples.original: Il est intelligent et, de plus, il est très travailleur.
examples.phonetic: /il ɛt ɛ̃teliʒɑ̃ e də plys il ɛ tʁɛ tʁavajœʁ/
examples.translation: He is intelligent and, moreover, he is very hardworking.
examples.note: 'De plus' is used in formal registers to add information. In Spanish, 'además' is more versatile; in French it is often preceded by a comma and can appear at the beginning of the sentence.

examples.original: Ce restaurant est cher, en revanche la qualité est excellente.
examples.phonetic: /sə ʁɛstoʁɑ̃ ɛ ʃɛʁ ɑ̃ ʁəvɑ̃ʃ la kalite ɛ ɛkselɑ̃t/
examples.translation: This restaurant is expensive, on the other hand the quality is excellent.
examples.note: 'En revanche' is used to contrast two aspects of the same thing. In Spanish, 'en cambio' has a similar use. Caution: do not use 'en contrepartie' in this context (that is more for exchanges).

examples.original: Il a raté le bus, pourtant il est parti tôt.
examples.phonetic: /il a ʁate lə bys puʁtɑ̃ il ɛ paʁti to/
examples.translation: He missed the bus, however (despite that) he left early.
examples.note: 'Pourtant' expresses opposition with a nuance of concession. It is often placed after the verb when it appears in the middle of the sentence. In spoken language it is more common than 'cependant'.

levels.label: Connecteurs de cause et de conséquence

examples.original: Il a plu toute la nuit ; par conséquent, le jardin est inondé.
examples.phonetic: /il a ply tut la nɥi paʁ kɔ̃sekɑ̃ lə ʒaʁdɛ̃ ɛ ɛnɔ̃de/
examples.translation: It rained all night; consequently, the garden is flooded.
examples.note: 'Par conséquent' is used in a formal register. In Spanish, 'por consiguiente' is more formal than 'así que'. It is a connector placed at the beginning of the second sentence.

examples.original: Elle est absente car elle est malade.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl ɛt apɑ̃t kaʁ ɛl ɛ malad/
examples.translation: She is absent because she is ill.
examples.note: 'Car' introduces an explanation and is more formal than 'parce que'. Unlike 'parce que', 'car' cannot answer the question 'pourquoi?' (why?) in an isolated answer.

examples.original: Puisque tu es là, aide-moi à porter ces cartons.
examples.phonetic: /pɥisk ty ɛ la ɛdmwa a pɔʁte se kaʁtɔ̃/
examples.translation: Since you are here, help me carry these boxes.
examples.note: 'Puisque' is used for a cause that the listener already knows or takes for granted. In Spanish, 'ya que' works the same. Do not use 'puisque' for new causes.

examples.original: D'abord, nous allons examiner le problème ; ensuite, nous proposerons des solutions.
examples.phonetic: /daʁbɔʁ nu zalɔ̃ ɛgzamine lə pʁɔblɛm ɑ̃sɥit nu pʁopozeʁɔ̃ de sɔlysjɔ̃/
examples.translation: First, we will examine the problem; then, we will propose solutions.
examples.note: 'D'abord' and 'ensuite' are discourse organizers that indicate sequence. In Spanish, 'primero' and 'luego' cover this function. They can be combined with 'enfin' (finally).

examples.original: Il a perdu son emploi, c'est-à-dire qu'il doit chercher un nouveau travail.
examples.phonetic: /il a pɛʁdy sɔ̃n ɑ̃plwa sɛtadiʁ kil dwa ʃɛʁʃe œ̃ nuvo tʁavaj/
examples.translation: He lost his job, that is to say, he must look for a new job.
examples.note: 'C'est-à-dire' is a reformulation connector that clarifies or explains something. In Spanish, 'es decir' is very similar. It is used both in speech and writing.

examples.original: Finalement, le projet a été accepté malgré les difficultés.
examples.phonetic: /finalmɑ̃ lə pʁoʒɛ a ete aksɛpte malɡʁe le difikylte/
examples.translation: Finally, the project was accepted despite the difficulties.
examples.note: 'Finalement' indicates the final point in a sequence or concludes an idea. Unlike 'enfin' which can also express relief, 'finalement' is used for conclusion.

title: Le langage de distanciamiento / Distancing language
bridge: In Spanish we use constructions like 'tiendo a', 'parece que', 'al parecer' to distance ourselves from a statement. In French, we have similar structures, but with important differences: the use of the subjunctive after 'il semble que' (whereas in Spanish we sometimes use the indicative), and the verb 'avoir tendance à' which requires 'à' before the infinitive (in Spanish 'tender a' without a preposition). We also have to watch the word order with adverbs like 'apparemment'. These differences are typical traps for Spanish speakers.
rule:
In French, to express distancing or mitigation, several structures are used:
- 'Avoir tendance à + infinitif' (to have a tendency to) for general habits or characteristics. E.g.: 'J'ai tendance à oublier les noms.'
- 'Il semble que + indicative/subjunctive' (it seems that). With 'il semble que' the subjunctive is normally used in formal French, but in negation or interrogation the subjunctive is used. However, with 'il me semble que' the indicative is used.
- 'Apparemment' (apparently) at the beginning of the sentence to indicate that the information is not certain.
- 'Il paraît que + indicative' (it seems that) is used with the indicative.
- The conditional of courtesy or rumor: 'On dirait que' (it would seem that) + indicative.
- Adverbs like 'peut-être' (perhaps) may require inversion if they appear at the beginning: 'Peut-être devrais-je...'.
It is important not to confuse 'il semble que' (subjunctive) with 'il me semble que' (indicative). Also remember that 'tendre à' (to tend to) does not take 'à' after the verb; instead it is 'tendre vers' or simply 'avoir tendance à'.

concept_examples.text: J'ai tendance à arriver en retard le lundi matin.
concept_examples.translation: I tend to arrive late on Monday mornings.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʒɛ tɑ̃dɑ̃s a aʁive ɑ̃ ʁetaʁ lə lœ̃di matɛ̃/

concept_examples.text: Il semble que le projet soit déjà terminé.
concept_examples.translation: It seems that the project is already finished.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il sɑ̃bl kə lə pʁɔʒɛ swa deʒa tɛʁmine/

concept_examples.text: Apparemment, elle a changé d'avis.
concept_examples.translation: Apparently, she changed her mind.
concept_examples.phonetic: /apaʁamɑ̃, ɛl a ʃɑ̃ʒe davi/

concept_examples.text: On dirait qu'il va pleuvoir.
concept_examples.translation: It seems that it will rain.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɔ̃ djɛ kil va pløvwaʁ/

common_error.wrong: Je tends à oublier les noms.
common_error.correct: J'ai tendance à oublier les noms.
common_error.correct_alt: Je tends à oublier les noms. (correcto pero menos común y más formal)
common_error.explanation: In Spanish, 'tiendo a olvidar los nombres' is literally translated as 'je tends à oublier', which is grammatically correct but not idiomatic. The most natural and common construction in French is 'avoir tendance à + infinitif'. Moreover, one must remember that 'tendre à' in French means 'to head towards' or 'to aim at', not 'to have the habit of'. To avoid this error, always use 'avoir tendance à'.

examples.original: J'ai tendance à parler trop vite quand je suis nerveux.
examples.phonetic: /ʒɛ tɑ̃dɑ̃s a paʁle tʁo vit kɑ̃ ʒɥi nɛʁvø/
examples.translation: I tend to speak too fast when I am nervous.
examples.note: It uses 'avoir tendance à' for general habits or behaviors. In Spanish we use 'tender a' without a preposition, but in French it requires 'à'.

examples.original: Elle a tendance à exagérer les histoires.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl a tɑ̃dɑ̃s a ɛgzaʒeʁe le istwaʁ/
examples.translation: She tends to exaggerate stories.
examples.note: Note the conjugation of 'avoir' and that 'tendance' is feminine.

levels.label: Il semble que / Il paraît que

examples.original: Il semble que les résultats soient positifs.
examples.phonetic: /il sɑ̃bl kə le ʁezylta swa pozitif/
examples.translation: It seems that the results are positive.
examples.note: After 'il semble que', the subjunctive (soient) is used. In Spanish, 'parece que' usually takes the indicative, so this is a common trap.

examples.original: Il paraît que Marie a trouvé un nouveau travail.
examples.phonetic: /il paʁɛ kə maʁi a tʁuve œ̃ nuvo tʁavaj/
examples.translation: It seems that Marie has found a new job.
examples.note: With 'il paraît que' the indicative (a trouvé) is used, unlike 'il semble que'. It is important to distinguish the two constructions.

examples.original: Apparemment, il n'y a pas de problème.
examples.phonetic: /apaʁamɑ̃, il ni a pa də pʁɔblɛm/
examples.translation: Apparently, there is no problem.
examples.note: Adverbs like 'apparemment' are placed at the beginning of the sentence to soften the statement.

examples.original: Peut-être devrais-je consulter un médecin.
examples.phonetic: /pøtɛtʁ dəvʁɛʒ kɔ̃sylte œ̃ medsɛ̃/
examples.translation: Perhaps I should consult a doctor.
examples.note: When 'peut-être' is at the beginning, subject inversion (devrais-je) occurs in formal register. In Spanish, 'quizás' + subjunctive, but here the conditional is used.
